question: Who has the power to "amend" the fundamental rights?
options: The Supreme Court can only review.
The President can only bring ordinances.
Parliament has to do so by amending the Constitution under Article 368.
solution: No part of the Constitution is 'unamendable', but Parliament cannot make any change which would destroy the basic spirit of the Constitution.

question: Who was the Chairman of the first Commission for Backward Classes (1953)?
solution: Kaka Kalelkar Commission had made several suggestions for identification of backward castes, but its recommendations were not implemented then.

question: What is the meaning of "begar" under Article 23?
solution: Article 23 prohibits human trafficking, forced labor and slavery. The Bonded Labor Abolition Act 1976 was enacted to implement this section.

question: Who called the “right to constitutional remedies” (Article 32) as the “soul and heart of the Constitution”?
solution: Article 32 gives the power to the citizens that if their fundamental rights are violated, they can directly approach the Supreme Court. The court can issue five types of writs.

question: What rights remain with a person arrested under “Preventive Detention”?
options: He should get an opportunity to make a representation against the order of detention so that he can explain himself.
Both options A and B are correct
He has the right to seek advice from a lawyer
The grounds for detention should be disclosed, although some facts may be suppressed in public interest.
solution: Preventive detention is a very harsh system. Therefore, the Constitution has made it mandatory under Article 22(5) that the State should inform the person of the grounds as soon as possible and give him an opportunity to appeal.

question: “Right against handcuffing” comes under which article?
solution: In the case Prem Shankar Shukla vs Delhi Administration, the court declared handcuffing without solid reason as unconstitutional.

question: How many types of "minorities" are there under Article 30?
options: Three types: religious, linguistic and ethnic
Four types: Economic basis also included
solution: Article 30 gives the right to minorities to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. The state will not discriminate against them while providing assistance.

question: What was the most important outcome of the Maneka Gandhi vs. Union of India (1978) case?
options: “Right to Privacy” is not a fundamental right
Confiscating passports is a discretionary power of the state
“Right to travel abroad” is part of Article 21
solution: This case cemented the concept of the 'Golden Triangle', in which Articles 14, 19 and 21 are considered interconnected.

question: The right against the practice of “untouchability” (Article 17) is available against whom?
solution: Article 17 is one of those rare rights which are absolute and against which the state or individual cannot give any argument. Its violation is a punishable offence.

question: Trick to remember the six freedoms granted under Article 19(1) What does the 'M' in "SAAMRO" stand for?
options: Move freely throughout the territory of India
solution: SAAMRO Trick: S-Speech, A-Assemble, A-Associations, M-Move, R-Reside, O-Occupation.

question: After what age does the right to “free education” under Article 21 cease to exist?
options: After completion of 14 years of age it ceases to be a fundamental right.
solution: The age group 6-14 years was chosen because it is the most important time for a child's mental development and basic literacy. After this, education goes into the realm of 'directive principles'.

question: Which statement is correct regarding Article 17 "Abolition of Untouchability"?
options: Only financial punishment can be given for following untouchability
The word 'untouchability' is not defined anywhere in the Constitution
This right is available only against the State
solution: Article 17 is an 'Absolute Right'. The Untouchability Offenses Act 1955 was later changed to 'Protection of Civil Rights Act 1976'.

question: What is the maximum period for which a person can be kept in preventive detention under Article 22(4) without the opinion of the Advisory Board?
solution: Preventive detention is done on the basis of suspicion so that future crime can be prevented. The advisory board should consist of persons of the rank of High Court judges to ensure impartiality of detention.

question: Article 28 of the Constitution allows "religious instruction" in which institutions?
options: Those institutions which are administered by the state but established by a trust
Institutions which are fully funded by the state
solution: Article 28 divides educational institutions into four categories and each has separate rules for religious education.

question: Article 33 gives the Parliament the power to restrict whose fundamental rights?
options: Armed forces, police and intelligence agencies
Only the rights of religious minorities are protected in Articles 29-30.
solution: Army soldiers do not have the same freedom of expression or association as the general public. This is necessary for national security.

question: 'Mandamus' writ cannot be issued against whom?
options: If the lower courts are not performing their duty, they may be issued.
This writ is not issued against the President and Governor of India for the performance of their duties against these high officials.
This writ applies to any government corporation in default of its official duties.
solution: 'Mandamesh' means "We order". It is issued when a public official fails to perform his legal duty. It cannot be issued against private persons.

question: Who has the power to impose the condition of "residence" under Article 16(3)?
options: This would be a violation of the powers possessed by the Chief Minister of the state.
The Governor can only give advice.
solution: At present only in states like Andhra Pradesh and Telangana the residence condition has been made mandatory by the Parliament for certain posts.

question: What is meant by “freedom of conscience” as used in Article 25?
options: Internal freedom to believe or not to believe in any religion
Unlimited right to take out religious processions on public roads
Forcibly converting others to propagate religion
Article 27 prohibits promotion of any particular religion by the state through taxes.
solution: Article 25 gives freedom not only to practice religion but also not to practice any religion (atheism). It is purely an individual right, whereas Article 26 is a collective or institutional right.

question: Which Article provides for the right of entry into "Public Restaurants/ Hotels"?
solution: Article 15(2) is one of those rights which is enforceable not only against the State, but also against the general public.

question: Which article of the Constitution deals with "Reservation in Promotion"?
solution: 16(4-A) empowers the State to provide reservation in promotion even for SC/ST if their representation is not adequate.

question: What is included in the prohibition of “Human Trafficking”?
options: Option A, B and C all
Buying and selling men, women and children as commodities is prohibited
Only bringing people from other countries
solution: Article 23 seeks to root out any form of human exploitation in India. The 'Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956' gives strength to this article.

question: What is the current stand of the Supreme Court regarding “Right to Die”?
options: Committing suicide is a fundamental right
Hunger strike is the right to die
Dying with dignity (Passive Euthanasia) is part of the right to life
solution: Passive euthanasia means that if someone is in a terminal condition, their life support can be removed. Aruna Ramchandra Shanbaug case had laid its foundation.

question: Within how much time is it mandatory to produce an arrested person before a Magistrate under Article 22?
solution: This right has been given to prevent arbitrary arrest and police torture. No one can be kept in custody after 24 hours without the permission of the magistrate.

question: Why is the right to approach the Supreme Court under Article 32 called the “right to constitutional remedies”?
options: Because it makes fundamental rights enforceable
Because it orders doctors to provide free treatment
Because it protects only the interests of lawyers
Because it gives the right to make changes in the Constitution, the power of amendment lies with the Parliament.
solution: Article 32 itself is a fundamental right. Dr. Ambedkar considered it the most important article of the Constitution because it is the protective shield of all other rights.

question: What was the approach of the Court in the case "A.K. Gopalan vs. State of Madras" (1950)?
options: It considered privacy as a fundamental right
solution: In the Gopalan case the 'procedure established by law' was interpreted literally. The Court said that Article 21 protects only against the arbitrariness of the executive and not the arbitrariness of the legislature.

question: Which article of the Indian Constitution gives the right to "establish educational institutions for minorities"?
solution: Article 30 can also be called the "Charter of Minorities". The State shall not discriminate while granting grants to these institutions on the ground that they are minority managed.

question: Article 26 Who has "freedom to manage religious affairs"?
options: Only individual citizens have individual rights in Article 25.
This is a group right for every religious sect or any part thereof.
solution: Under this, religious institutions can own their movable and immovable properties, establish institutions and manage their religious activities themselves.

question: Who has the right to suspend the implementation of fundamental rights?
options: Parliament can make amendments, but immediate adjournment is the order of the President.
Under Article 359, the President can adjourn them in case of emergency (except 20, 21).
solution: The President can also suspend Article 32 (right to go to court), thereby rendering other rights ineffective.

question: Who is not included in the word “Hindu” as per Article 25(2)(b)?
solution: Article 25 talks about opening of Hindu religious institutions to 'all classes of Hindus', where the definition of the word Hindu is broad.

question: Under "Cultural Rights" (Article 29) on what grounds cannot the State refuse admission to an educational institution?
options: Admission may be withheld on the basis of economic status and educational qualification.
Article 29(2) specifically prohibits discrimination on these four grounds: religion, race, caste and language.
solution: If there is a government aided school, it cannot say that only 'Hindi' speaking or only 'Hindu' children will study here. He has to give equal opportunity to everyone.

question: Where is the concept of “Procedure Established by Law” taken from under Article 21?
solution: Initially A.K. In the Gopalan case (1950), the court said that if the government has taken someone's life by making a law, then the court will not interfere. But after the Maneka Gandhi case (1978), the court also adopted 'due process of law'.

question: Which Article of the “Bonded Labor Abolition Act, 1976” was enacted to give effect to?
solution: Article 23 ends the evil practices like 'begar' and 'bonded labour' that have been going on in India for centuries. This right is available to both citizens and foreigners and applies against both the State and private individuals.

question: What additional grounds for discrimination in public employment are included under Article 16(2) that were not in Article 15?
solution: Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in public appointments. However, Article 16(3) gives the Parliament the power to impose 'residence' conditions for certain jobs.

question: Which two rights does an arrested person have under Article 22(1)?
options: Right to go free without warrant
Right to free food and entertainment in jail
Police have the right to punish
Right to know the reason for arrest and right to seek advice from a lawyer
solution: Article 22 gives protective rights so that there is no torture in police custody. He should be immediately told why he has been arrested and he should get legal aid.

question: Under which article “Free Legal Aid” and “Right to Speedy Trial” are considered fundamental rights?
solution: In the case of Hussainara Khatoon vs. State of Bihar, speedy trial was considered a part of Article 21. This is very important for the undertrials lodged in the jail.

question: What is the literal meaning of 'Habeas Corpus' writ?
solution: If the police or any other person illegally detains someone, the court orders that the person be physically produced before the court so that the legality of his detention can be examined. ADM Jabalpur case is related to this.

question: What type of education has been made compulsory under the “Right to Education” Act?
options: Primary and Secondary Education (6 to 14 years)
solution: The 86th Constitutional Amendment 2002 made education a fundamental right. Under this, it is the duty of the state to ensure free and compulsory education for children of 6 to 14 years of age.

question: According to Article 27, what is the difference between "fee" and "tax" collected for religious functions?
options: Both are sources of income for the state and can apply to any religion
Taxes cannot be levied to promote a particular religion, while fees may be levied for facilities
Both Fees and Taxes are strictly prohibited
Tax can be taken but not fee
solution: Article 27 ensures that the public treasury (tax money) is not used for the propagation of any one religion. However, it is legal to charge 'fees' for the facilities provided at pilgrimage sites as they are taken in return for a service.

question: For whom can the State make special provisions under Article 15(3)?
solution: Although Article 15 prohibits discrimination, Article 15(3) empowers the State to make special rules for the upliftment of weaker sections of the society such as women and children.

question: What is the meaning of 'Doctrine of Waiver'?
options: Denial of rights to foreign citizens
The government can withdraw the rights at any time
Automatic termination of rights during emergency
No citizen can give up fundamental rights on his own will
solution: In America, citizens can give up their rights, but in India the judiciary has held that the people here should not give up their rights due to their ignorance or poverty, hence the 'principle of renunciation' does not apply in India.

question: Ending the practice of "beggar" comes under which right?
solution: The right against exploitation (Articles 23-24) is designed to protect the most vulnerable in society (such as workers and children).

question: Article 19(1)(f) “Right to property” is now included in which Article?
solution: After the 44th Amendment in 1978, the right to property was removed from the list of fundamental rights so that the goals of land reforms and socialism could be achieved.

question: Why are fundamental rights considered a “boon” for Indian citizens?
options: All the above reasons are correct
Because they protect the individual from the autocratic power of the state
Because these are protected and enforceable by the judiciary
Because they ensure minimum conditions for the physical and moral development of the individual
solution: Fundamental rights are not just words written on paper, but they are living rights that guarantee every citizen to live with dignity. These establish India as a true democratic republic.

question: When can the writ of “Mandamus” not be used?
options: When the duty is discretionary and not mandatory
When a contractual obligation is to be enforced
When the Chief Justice of the High Court is acting in a judicial capacity, this writ is not issued against him.
solution: 'Mandamus' means "We command". It is an active writ which awakens the sleeping officer. It cannot be issued against private individuals, the President or Governors.

question: What reasonable restrictions can be imposed on the right to “peaceful assembly” (Article 19(1)(b))?
options: In the interest of sovereignty and integrity of India
To stop criticism of a political party
Both options A and B are correct
solution: The right to hold conferences, but it must be “without arms.” The administration can impose Section 144 to maintain law and order, which is a reasonable restriction on this right.

question: The main objective of the fundamental rights is “to create a government of law and not of persons” – This statement is associated with which concept?
solution: Fundamental rights impose 'negative constraints' on the powers of the state. They tell what the government cannot do. This ensures that the country will not be run by the whims of any one person, but by the Constitution and the law.

question: What is the meaning of “Forced Labour”?
options: Working only due to physical compulsion
Working at low wages due to economic compulsion (poverty)
Doing a government job is a service.
solution: In the People's Union for Democratic Rights (PUDR) case, the court said that not paying minimum wages is also a violation of Article 23.

question: In which educational institutions "religious education" is completely banned under Article 28?
options: Institutions established by trusts which are administered by the state
solution: India's secularism means that the state has no religion of its own and will not allow government educational institutions to become centers of religious propaganda.

question: In which case “Right to Shelter” was considered a fundamental right?
options: Olga Tellis vs. Bombay Municipal Corporation
solution: The court said that right to life means having a roof over the head, otherwise life would have no meaning.

question: In which case was “Right to Privacy” declared a fundamental right?
solution: Right to privacy is now a basic right of a citizen. This includes the individual's rights to personal data, choice and privacy.

question: Which article of the Constitution compensates for the loss of rights during "Martial Law"?
solution: Under Article 34, Parliament gives protection to those military officers who have taken drastic steps to restore law and order.

question: The right to “free education” is now a fundamental right up to what age?
options: The state is not obliged to provide higher education up to graduation.
solution: Through the 86th amendment, education was included in Part Three so that every child can achieve basic literacy.

question: Why is “Equality before Law” considered a negative concept?
options: Because it reduces the power of the judiciary
Because it violates the rights of the poor
Because it creates anarchy in the society
Because it denotes the absence of special privileges in favor of any person
solution: This concept, taken from Britain, believes that no one is above the law. However, complete equality is not possible, so 'equal protection of laws' (positive concept) has also been adopted from the US.

question: When and by which amendment was the right to property removed from the list of fundamental rights?
solution: Right to property is now a legal right in Part XII under Article 300-A. Now if the State takes someone's property, it can take it only by right of law, but the citizen cannot claim it as a fundamental right.

question: What is included in the word 'law' under Article 13?
solution: If any government order abridges the fundamental rights, it can be challenged under Article 13.

question: What is not included in “freedom of speech and expression”?
options: ❌ Right to strike (this is not included)
Right to fly the flag (this includes)
solution: To strike is not a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a); It can be controlled as a legal right. Hoisting the flag and remaining silent (Emmanuel v. State of Kerala) are forms of expression.

question: “Right to Environment” is a fundamental right under which article?
solution: M.C. In the case of Mehta vs. Union of India, the Court considered the right to pollution-free water and air as an integral part of Article 21.

question: What is the difference between the writ powers of the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High Court (Article 226)?
options: The power of the Supreme Court is more extensive
The jurisdiction of the High Court (Writ Jurisdiction) is more extensive
Both options A and C are correct
Supreme Court cannot refuse to issue writs
solution: SC can issue writs for the whole of India, while HC can issue writs only for its own territory. But HC can also give writs for legal rights, which SC cannot give.

question: “Quo-Warranto” writ cannot be issued against whom?
options: As against ministerial office or private office
This writ is suitable to test the validity of public posts against the Municipal Corporation Chairman.
solution: Quo warrant means "by what warrant or authority". It prevents a person from usurping public office illegally. It is not issued against the post of minister because it is an executive post.

question: Under which articles the fundamental rights cannot be suspended during emergency?
solution: After the 44th Constitutional Amendment in 1978, a provision was made that the rights given under Articles 20 and 21 will remain protected even during emergency. This has been done to ensure the safety of lives of the citizens.

question: What is the main purpose of the writ of certiorari?
options: To order an officer to do work
To release a person from jail
To set aside the wrong decision of the lower court
solution: A writ of certiorari is issued when a lower court has ruled beyond its jurisdiction or made a clear error of law.

question: What was the purpose of Article 13(4) which was added by the 24th Amendment?
options: Giving more powers to the President
Declaring that constitutional amendment is not "law" and cannot be challenged
solution: Parliament added Article 13(4) so ​​that they could amend the fundamental rights and the court could not abrogate them by citing Article 13. However, later the principle of 'Basic Structure' came into existence in the Kesavananda Bharti case.

question: Who has the power to make laws regarding fundamental rights?
options: State legislatures cannot amend fundamental rights or decide penalties related to them.
Only the President can issue ordinances, it is the function of Parliament to make laws.
solution: This arrangement has been made so that there is uniformity in the fundamental rights and the penalties related to them throughout India.

question: How many judges comprised the bench that made "Right to Privacy" a fundamental right?
solution: The 9 judges unanimously held that the right to privacy is an integral part of life and personal liberty under Article 21.

question: What is the maximum period of "Preventive Detention" under Article 22?
solution: Punitive detention occurs after a crime has been committed, while preventive detention occurs to prevent a crime from occurring in the future. India is one of the few democratic countries in the world where there is a provision for preventive detention even during peace time.

question: What is the decision of the Supreme Court regarding 'Awards' under Article 18?
options: These awards have now been discontinued
These should be given only to army personnel
Bharat Ratna and Padma awards cannot be used with the name
These awards violate the right to equality
solution: In the Balaji Raghavan case (1996), the court clarified that there is a difference between 'title' and 'award'. There is no harm in taking an award, but displaying it like a feudal title is wrong.

question: Which article of the Constitution prohibits "human trafficking and forced labour"?
solution: Article 23 is available to both citizens and non-citizens. This also includes immoral trafficking of women and children.

question: On what grounds can "religious freedom" be restricted under Article 25?
options: Tax cannot be imposed for propagation of religion only if tax is not paid.
Only in opposition to other religions
solution: Article 25 grants freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practice and propagate religion. This also includes the right of the Sikh community to wear 'Kripan'.

question: In which year was “Right to Privacy” recognized as a fundamental right?
solution: The right to privacy is now an integral part of Article 21. This means that the state cannot interfere in a person's private life, data and personal decisions unless there is a valid legal basis. The Puttaswamy case overturned earlier decisions (Kharak Singh and MP Sharma).

question: What historic decision did the Supreme Court give in the Indira Sawhney vs. Union of India (1992) case?
options: The total limit of reservation should not exceed 50%
Reservation in promotion should be mandatory
Reservation can be done only on the basis of caste
solution: This case is also known as 'Mandal Case'. In this, the Court also made it clear that reservation would be only in initial appointment and not in promotion (although this was changed by later amendments).

question: According to Article 27, for which work the state cannot impose 'tax'?
options: Fee may be imposed for providing facilities to pilgrims, but not tax.
Asking for donations for temple renovation
To promote or nurture any particular religion
solution: Article 27 ensures that the state remains neutral towards all religions. There is a difference between 'tax' and 'fee'; Fees may be charged for services, but not taxes.

question: Under Article 24, employment of children below which age in hazardous industries is prohibited?
solution: The purpose of Article 24 is to protect the health of children and their childhood. Later, by amending the laws, there has been a ban on employing children in any commercial work so that their education is not affected.

question: Where is the word "minority" defined in the Constitution?
solution: Minorities are identified on linguistic and religious basis. The Central Government has so far declared 6 communities as minorities at the national level.

question: Who is considered the “Guardian” of fundamental rights?
solution: Article 32 makes the Supreme Court and Article 226 makes the High Court the protector of rights.

question: When is 'Quo-Warranto' writ used?
options: When the lower court has given a wrong decision
When someone is prevented from going abroad, there is a remedy under Habeas Corpus or Article 21.
When the police are not arresting anyone, there is a writ of mandamus.
When the validity of a person's claim to a public office has to be checked
solution: It means "by what authority". Any interested person (not necessarily aggrieved) can apply for this writ. It cannot be issued against private offices.

question: In which historical case was the principle of 'Judicial Review' first established?
solution: Article 13 is the basis of judicial review in India. It gives the power to the judiciary to declare illegal any law which violates Part Three (Fundamental Rights).

question: Which new sections were added by the 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019?
solution: The 103rd Amendment made 'economic backwardness' the basis for reservation for the first time. Under this, reservation is given to those people who are not included in SC, ST or OBC category.

question: Who is immune from arrest in civil or criminal cases under Article 14?
options: Only foreign ambassadors are exempt, but the President and Governors are major exceptions.
No punitive action can be initiated against the President and the Governor while they are in office.
solution: The right to equality is not absolute. The President, Governors, foreign sovereigns, ambassadors and MPs/MLAs (for speeches made within the House) have certain exemptions from Article 14.

question: What is the main exception to the “Quo-Warranto” writ?
options: This can be issued only by the President
This is only against police officers
It cannot be issued against a minister's office or private entities
It is issued only when a person has died
solution: If a person has been made the manager of a company wrongfully, you cannot go to court (under Article 32). But if someone has wrongly become a judge or collector, then writ of quo warranto will be applicable.

question: What is this principle called that the limit of “backlog” vacancies under Article 16(4-B) can exceed 50%?
options: What is this principle called, under which the limit of “backlog” vacancies can exceed 50%? A) Carry Forward Rule
solution: It was added by the 81st Constitutional Amendment in 2000 so that vacant seats belonging to reserved categories can be filled even if the total reservation for that year crosses 50%.

question: What is the difference between "Due Process of Law" and "Procedure established by law"?
options: All the above statements are true
The established process only sees whether the law is passed correctly or not
Due process also examines the fairness and reasonableness of the law
Now both are coordinated in the Indian Constitution
solution: Article 21 says "procedure established by law". Earlier it meant that Parliament could make whatever law it wanted. But now the Court says that the law should be "Just, Fair and Reasonable".

question: After which famous case Article 15(4) was added by the First Constitutional Amendment (1951)?
options: Champakam Dorairajan vs. State of Madras
solution: Article 15(4) empowers the State to make special provisions for the social and educational upliftment of the Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST).

question: According to Article 24, children below how many years of age cannot be employed in factories or in hazardous work?
solution: Article 24 protects the childhood and health of children. Following the 2016 amendment, children are prevented from working in any occupation except their family business (after school).

question: “Creamy Layer” is identified for which group?
solution: In the Indira Sawhney case (1992), the Court said that the benefits of OBC reservation should actually reach the needy. Those who have progressed a lot economically and socially should be kept out of the race for reservation.

question: Which Article exempts "foreign ambassadors" from being arrested in India?
solution: Diplomats are exempt from host country laws due to the Vienna Convention and international laws.

question: Which title is not prohibited under Article 18 "End of Titles"?
options: Titles received from foreign states without permission
solution: In 1996, in the Balaji Raghavan case, the Supreme Court said that Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan etc. are 'awards' and not 'titles'. Therefore, they cannot be used as suffix/prefix in front or behind the name.

question: According to Article 15, on what grounds does the state prohibit discrimination?
options: Religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
solution: Article 15(1) states that the State shall not discriminate against any citizen 'solely' on these five grounds. Article 15(2) also prohibits private individuals from discriminating in public places (e.g. hotels, shops, wells).

question: Which article is the main basis of "Rule of Law"?
solution: A.V. According to Dicey, 'rule of law' means absence of arbitrary power and equality of all before the law.

question: By which amendment reservation in educational institutions (including private institutions) was added under Article 15(5)?
solution: This article gives the state the power to implement reservation in all private colleges except minority institutions.

question: Which Article of the “Right to Equality” (Articles 14-18) prohibits the “exercise of offices or titles”?
solution: Article 18 is essential for the establishment of democracy where all citizens are equal. Hereditary titles like 'Rai Bahadur' or 'Raja' are against the principles of equality, so they were abolished.

question: What is not included in the right to “Propagate Religion” under Article 25(1)?
options: Explaining the tenets of your religion
It is a constitutional right to preach within the scope of public peace.
solution: In Stanislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh, the Court held that the "right of publicity" does not include the "right to effect change" as it infringes the freedom of conscience of another person.

question: Under which article "wearing of kirpans by Sikhs" is considered a part of religious freedom?
solution: It is clearly written in the explanation of Article 25 that wearing a kirpan and carrying it will be considered a part of following the Sikh religion. It is an integral part of their religious identity.

question: What is the difference between Martial Law (Article 34) and National Emergency (Article 352)?
options: Martial law applies to the entire country
Martial law affects only the fundamental rights, while the emergency also affects the government and centre-state relations.
Emergency is imposed only by the Army
Courts remain active during martial law
solution: Martial law (military rule) is imposed to restore law and order in extraordinary situations. During this, Parliament can give legal recognition to those military actions which would have been illegal in normal times.

question: Article 31-B is related to which schedule which was created to protect it from judicial review?
options: The Ninth Schedule was added by the First Amendment (1951).
solution: Article 31-B states that if a law is put in the Ninth Schedule, it cannot be challenged on the grounds of violation of fundamental rights (although review is now possible after 2007).

question: What can the State do as an exception to “forced labour”?
options: Can impose compulsory service (such as army or social service) for public purposes
The state cannot do anything like this, it is completely prohibited
Can only make prisoners work without money
Can make work only from minorities
solution: Article 23(2) says that the State may impose compulsory service for public purposes, but while doing so, it shall not discriminate on grounds of religion, race, caste or class.

question: “Right to clean drinking water” comes under which article?
solution: The Supreme Court has held in several judgments that basic amenities like water, air and electricity come under Article 21.

question: In which case "Right to Speedy Trial" was considered a fundamental right under Article 21?
options: A.K. Gopalan vs. State of Madras
Hussainara Khatoon vs. State of Bihar
Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India
solution: In the Hussainara Khatoon case (1979), the Court held that if there is excessive delay in the trial of an accused, it is a violation of his right to life (Article 21). Justice delayed is justice denied.

question: On what grounds has the word "minority" been used under Article 29?
options: Only on the basis of caste
On the basis of economic condition
solution: Article 29 is not just for minorities, but for "any section of citizens". However, Article 30 specifically talks about minorities.

question: Under which article restrictions on fundamental rights are imposed during "Martial Law"?
solution: The concept of martial law has been taken from Britain. It differs from a national emergency as it may apply only to a smaller area. 'Martial law' is not defined in the Indian Constitution.

question: Under which article "Freedom of the Press" is considered a fundamental right?
solution: In Romesh Thapar vs. State of Madras (1950), the Supreme Court clarified that freedom of the press is the basis of democracy and is part of Article 19(1)(a).

question: “Self-incrimination” is prohibited in which article?
solution: This means that the statement given in police custody is not valid in the court unless the accused makes it voluntarily in front of a magistrate.

question: In which case was "Right to Internet" considered a part of Article 19?
options: Anuradha Bhasin vs Union of India
solution: The court said that the Internet is the main medium of trade and expression in today's era, hence shutting it down indefinitely is a violation of fundamental rights.

question: Under Article 28, in which type of educational institution religious education can be imparted on voluntary basis?
options: Institutions fully funded by the state
Only private colleges where the state has no role
Institutions aided or recognized by the state
solution: Article 28 ensures secular education system. Religious education is completely prohibited in government schools, while in other private or aided institutions it is dependent on the individual's wishes.

question: In what areas can the right to “Move Freely” be restricted?
options: On public health and safety grounds
To protect the interests of tribal areas, there may be a ban on visiting the tribal areas so that their culture and security is not affected by the arrival of outsiders.
Both options A and B are correct
Only to go to other countries
solution: A citizen of India can move anywhere, but special permission is required to visit 'Inner Line Permit' (ILP) areas or restricted military areas.

question: What three conditions have been stated by the Supreme Court for being a "Religious Denomination"?
options: Must be recognized by the state
A group of persons having common beliefs, a common organization and a distinct name
There need only be a very large population
Must be of foreign origin only
solution: Ramakrishna Mission and Anand Marg are considered sects. Article 26 gives these sects autonomy to run their institutions and manage property.

question: Article 31-C was added by which amendment which gives priority to certain directive principles over fundamental rights?
solution: Article 31-C says that if the State makes a law to prevent centralization of wealth and for equitable distribution of resources, it cannot be repealed on the ground that it curtails equality or freedom.

question: By which Prime Minister were the recommendations of the Mandal Commission (1979) implemented in 1990?
options: 27% reservation in government jobs was announced for. B) Morarji Desai
solution: The Mandal Commission had found that about 52% of India's population was Other Backward Classes (OBC), so they recommended 27% reservation.

question: Under Article 35, why does Parliament have the “exclusive power” to make laws with respect to fundamental rights?
options: So that there is uniformity in the fundamental rights and punishment for their violation in the entire country.
Because state legislatures are not competent
Because fundamental rights are only against the central government
solution: If the punishment for untouchability is 2 years in Tamil Nadu and 2 days in Punjab, it would be unfair. That is why Article 35 has given the power to make punishments and rules only to the Parliament.

question: Who is not included in the definition of 'State' under Article 12?
options: The Parliament and Government of India are clearly considered to be part of the State in Article 12.
solution: Article 12 defines the term 'State' to make it clear against whom the fundamental rights will apply. It includes the Central Government, Parliament, State Governments, Legislative Assemblies and all local or other statutory bodies.

question: 'Doctrine of Eclipse' is related to which article?
solution: According to Article 13(1), if any law is made before the coming into force of the Constitution and is repugnant to the fundamental rights, it shall be 'void' to the extent to which it is repugnant. That law remains dormant and may be reactivated if opposition to it is quelled by a future constitutional amendment.

question: How many fundamental rights were provided in the original Constitution?
solution: Originally there were 7 rights in the Constitution: equality, freedom, against exploitation, religious freedom, culture and education, right to property and constitutional remedies. The right to property was removed by the 44th amendment.

question: When is the protection of Article 20(2) “double jeopardy” not available?
options: In case of departmental or administrative proceedings, if the office has suspended you, it is not considered as 'court punishment'.
Only if there is both a departmental investigation and court punishment, a person may have to face both.
solution: If a government servant is caught taking bribe, he can be jailed (by the court) and even fired from the job (by the department). This will not be considered double punishment.

question: What articles are included in the "Golden Triangle"?
solution: In the Maneka Gandhi case, the court said that these three articles are not separate from each other; If a law violates Article 21, it must also satisfy the criteria of Articles 14 and 19.

question: By which amendment was the right to form "Cooperative Societies" added under Article 19(1)(c)?
solution: Now citizens can not only form associations or unions, but forming cooperative societies is also their fundamental right.

question: What kind of secularism does Article 27, which prohibits "Religious Tax", promote?
options: The State shall grant equal grants to all religions
The state will completely interfere in matters of religion
The state will have its own state religion
The state will not favor any religion and will not use tax money for religious propagation
solution: Article 27 ensures that the money of minorities does not go to promote the majority religion and vice versa. This strengthens the secular character of the state.

question: “Habeas Corpus” writ can be used against whom?
options: This writ can be issued against both public authority and private person if any person or police imprisons someone illegally.
solution: Habeas Corpus literally means "submission of the body". This is the greatest guarantee of individual freedom. This writ applies if someone is kept in the police station for more than 24 hours without the permission of the magistrate.

question: What is the meaning of 'Equal Protection of Laws' under Article 14?
options: Giving the power to make laws to the judiciary is against the separation of powers.
To govern everyone with the same law, no matter what the circumstances, would be against the real objective of equality.
Treating people in similar circumstances equally
Making separate laws for the rich would be discriminatory.
solution: Equal protection of the laws means that if two people have different circumstances, they may be classified differently. The foundation of the test of 'reasonable classification' was laid in the Anwar Ali Sarkar case (1952).

question: What is the main difference between “Prohibition” and “Certiorari” writ?
options: Certiorari can be issued only by the Supreme Court
Prohibition can be against private persons
Writs are only against the police
Prohibition is issued during the proceedings, while certiorari is for 'stopping' and certiorari is for 'cancelling'
solution: Prohibition means "to refuse", it prevents the lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction. Certiorari means "to be fully informed", it is to bring the matter up by overturning the wrong decision.

question: Is “Right to Work” a fundamental right?
options: Yes, it is part of Article 21
Yes, it is part of Article 19
No, it is a Directive Principle (DPSP)
solution: In the Olga Tellis case, the Court held that the right to livelihood is a part of the right to life, but the state can provide work only according to its economic capacity.

question: Under which article 'Right to Information' (RTI) is considered a fundamental right?
solution: In Raj Narayan v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1975) the Court held that people are entitled to know about governance. Later in 2005 the RTI Act was passed.

question: “Quo-Warranto” writ can be filed by whom?
options: Any citizen can bring it only by government lawyer.
By any interested person, even if he is not aggrieved
solution: Since it is to maintain the dignity of public office, the Court can inquire into it on the petition of any citizen.

question: Which writ is issued only against judicial or quasi-judicial bodies?
solution: 'Prohibition' is to stop the proceedings (stop), while 'prohibition' is to set aside a wrong decision or transfer the case (deferring).

question: Which article enshrines the right to "arm-free and peaceful assembly"?
solution: This right is also not unlimited. If it disturbs public order, it can be stopped under Section 144 (CrPC).

question: When can the "right to constitutional remedies" (Article 32) be suspended?
options: During President's rule, there is no suspension of rights when there is an emergency in the state.
Anytime on the advice of the Prime Minister
By order of the President under Article 359 during national emergency.
solution: Article 32 can be suspended only when there is a clear provision for it in the Constitution (like Articles 358 and 359).

question: Which part of the Indian Constitution is called the "Magna Carta of India"?
solution: Fundamental rights are those rights which are essential for the all-round development of the citizens. Part Three of the Indian Constitution is called the "Magna Carta of India" because of its importance. These rights are justiciable, which means that if they are violated, they can go directly to court.

question: Who is called the father of 'Public Interest Litigation' (PIL) in India?
solution: The concept of PIL has been taken from America. Its objective is to provide justice to those people of the society who cannot reach the court themselves. Hussainara Khatoon vs. State of Bihar (1979) is considered to be the first PIL case.

question: Which fundamental rights are available only to Indian citizens and not to foreigners?
solution: Freedom from discrimination (15), equality in employment (16), six freedoms (19), and cultural rights of minorities (29-30) are reserved only for Indians.

question: What does Article 31-A of the Constitution relate to?
options: Zamindari abolition and land reform laws were added to it by the First Amendment.
This is Article 30 regarding the rights of minorities.
solution: Article 31-A says that land reform laws cannot be challenged on the ground of violation of Articles 14 and 19.

question: What are "cultural and educational rights" (Articles 29-30) primarily intended for?
options: To protect the unique identity of the weaker and minority sections of the society
Only for private schools of rich people
Only for those who want to speak Sanskrit
solution: There are many religions and languages ​​in India. If the majority imposes its language on others, diversity will disappear. That is why the Constitution has given minorities the special right to save their culture.

question: What type of democracy is envisaged to implement fundamental rights?
solution: Fundamental rights limit the powers of the state and provide freedom to citizens, thereby creating a healthy political environment. This is called political democracy.

question: “Right to Education” under Article 21-A is for which age group of children?
solution: It was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment 2002. The Mohini Jain and Unnikrishnan case had paved the way for this amendment by linking education with the right to life (Article 21).

question: According to Article 15(2), where is discrimination prohibited?
options: This section does not apply to private property at private residences and private parties.
Shops, public restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment
Both options A and B are correct
On wells, ponds, bathing ghats and roads
solution: Article 15(2) strikes at the roots of casteism and untouchability. This right is available not only against the state but also against the general public (private individuals).

question: “Clean environment” and “freedom from noise pollution” are part of which fundamental right?
solution: The Court held in 'MC Mehta' and other cases that the right to life is not only to breathe, but also to live in a dignified and healthy environment. This includes rules like ban on loudspeakers at night.

question: What is true regarding “Protection of interests of minorities” (Article 29)?
options: It is only for religious minorities
It has only the right to establish educational institutions
It is only for foreign citizens
It can apply to any section of citizens (including the majority)
solution: Article 29(1) says that any class of citizens residing in any part of India has the right to preserve their language, script and culture. Article 29(2) prohibits admission to educational institutions on grounds of religion or caste.

question: From which year the "Right to Education" (RTE) Act came into effect?
solution: To give effect to Article 21-A, Parliament passed the 'Right to Education Act 2009'.

question: Which article is called "Protection in respect of conviction"?
solution: Article 20 has three parts: protection from ex post facto litigation, immunity from double punishment and protection from testifying against oneself.

question: The prohibition of “ex-post-facto law” under Article 20 applies only to which laws?
solution: If you did something today which is not a legal offence, then the government cannot make a new law tomorrow and punish you for today's action.

question: The case "Shreya Singhal vs. Union of India" deals with the interpretation of which Article?
solution: Shreya Singhal Case (2015) is a milestone for freedom of expression on the internet. The Court held that arresting someone for posting on social media is a violation of Article 19(1)(a).

question: What is the new name of "Untouchability Offenses Act, 1955"?
solution: Under this law, a person following untouchability can also be prevented from contesting elections.

question: In which cases Article 35 gives special power to Parliament to make laws?
options: Both options A and B are correct
To give effect to Articles 16(3), 32(3), 33 and 34
In the case of deciding punishment for violation of fundamental rights, the punishment for untouchability or forced labor will be decided by the Parliament only.
To make laws on the subjects of the State List
solution: State legislatures do not have the power to decide punishment to enforce fundamental rights. This power rests only with the Parliament so that the nature of punishment remains uniform throughout the country.

question: After which case the principle of "Due Process of Law" was established in the Indian Constitution?
solution: 'Due process of law' means that the law should not only be made through constitutional process, but it should also be reasonable, fair and just.

question: Which statement is true regarding the nature of fundamental rights?
options: These can be suspended only during an emergency
These are not absolute and reasonable restrictions can be imposed
These are sacred and their violation is not possible under any circumstances.
These are permanent and cannot be changed
solution: Fundamental rights protect citizens from the tyranny of the state. These are justifiable but not absolute. The framers of the Constitution have provided for "reasonable restrictions" to strike a balance between individual liberty and social control.

question: How are the rights enjoyed by minorities under Article 30 different from those enjoyed by the majority?
options: They are not bound to follow government rules in their institutions
They can establish and administer educational institutions of their choice
They get more grants from the state
They do not need to pay any tax
solution: Article 30 empowers minorities through education to maintain their culture and identity. The State shall not discriminate while granting assistance merely on the ground that the institution is under the management of a minority.

question: What is the main difference between “constitutional remedies” (Article 32) and “legal remedies”?
options: Constitutional remedy is only for the rich
Article 32 itself is a fundamental right, while other legal remedies are derived from common laws
solution: If an ordinary law takes away any of your legal rights (such as breach of contract), you will go through the normal process. But if fundamental rights are taken away, you can directly go to SC, this power is given by Article 32.

question: What is meant by protection from “ex-post-facto law” under Article 20?
options: Foreign nationals cannot be punished in India
No one can be compelled to testify against himself
Punishment cannot be given twice for the same crime
A person cannot be punished for an act which was not a crime at the time of its commission.
solution: Article 20(1) ensures that the State cannot punish innocent citizens by retroactively applying a new law. This protection extends only to criminal laws, not civil or tax laws.

question: What is not included in the period of 24 hours under Article 22(2)?
solution: This protection ensures that police do not keep someone without legal supervision for long periods of time.
